title: Measured silent defects in widely used npm packages
note: Every entry was reproduced locally against the version named in `measuredAgainst`. `reproduce` is runnable as written. Nothing here is inferred from documentation or issue trackers.

findings.headline: bytes.parse('5MiB') returns 5
findings.detail: It reads the leading number and ignores an IEC unit entirely. An express body limit written limit: '5MiB' becomes a five-byte limit, so every request is rejected. bytes is what body-parser uses.
findings.affectsYouIf: you pass a size string containing KiB, MiB, GiB or TiB to anything backed by bytes — express/body-parser limits, multer, or your own config
findings.workaround: Use a plain byte count, or a parser that understands IEC units.

findings.headline: bytes and bytes-iec return different numbers for the same string
findings.detail: bytes reads 1MB as 1,048,576; bytes-iec reads it as 1,000,000. They are 2.4% apart at kB, 4.9% at MB, 7.4% at GB and 10% at TB, always in the direction of allowing more than was written. Neither says which convention it used, so swapping one for the other silently resizes every limit already deployed.
findings.affectsYouIf: you have both in a dependency tree, or you are migrating between them
findings.workaround: Write IEC units (MiB) when you mean binary sizes; they are unambiguous.

findings.headline: bytes answers unreadable input with a number
findings.detail: Measured over 17 unreadable strings, bytes returned a number for 13 of them rather than refusing.
findings.reproduce:
const b = require('bytes');
b.parse('1,5MB')     // 1
b.parse('10 MB 5')   // 10
b.parse('0x10MB')    // 0
b.parse('1XB')       // 1
findings.affectsYouIf: a size can come from a human-edited config file or an environment variable
findings.workaround: Validate the string before parsing it.

findings.headline: flat destroys a value when a key contains the delimiter
findings.detail: Flattening and unflattening is only useful if it round-trips. A key containing a dot collides with the path separator and one of the two values is lost. Keys with dots are ordinary: i18n message ids, hostnames, metric names, CSV headers.
findings.reproduce:
const {flatten, unflatten} = require('flat');
unflatten(flatten({'a.b': 1, a: {b: 2}}))  // {a: {b: 2}} — the first value is gone
findings.affectsYouIf: you flatten objects whose keys can contain a dot, a bracket or a backslash
findings.workaround: Escape the keys yourself, or use a flattener that does.

findings.headline: flat turns an object with numeric keys into a sparse array
findings.detail: There is no option that keeps both: the default turns numeric-keyed objects into arrays, and {object: true} turns every array into an object. Across 25 fixtures the default kept 13 and {object: true} kept 11.
findings.affectsYouIf: your objects can be keyed by ids, indices or anything numeric
findings.workaround: None within flat; the trade is structural.

findings.headline: deserializeError is exponential in the depth of the cause chain
findings.detail: 0.4 ms at depth 5, 10.6 ms at 10, 339 ms at 15 and 11 seconds at depth 20, on a payload of 6.6 KB. In destroyCircular, `cause` is walked once in the Object.keys loop and again in the errorProperties loop, and seen.delete(from) makes cycle detection path-based rather than memoised, so the two paths compound to 2^depth. Serializing is fast because `cause` is non-enumerable on a real Error; a JSON round trip makes it enumerable, which is exactly the worker-to-main-thread path the library exists for.
findings.affectsYouIf: you wrap errors with `cause` through several layers and send them across a boundary as JSON
findings.workaround: Cap the cause chain before serialising, or use a serialiser that handles errors iteratively.

findings.headline: parse-duration reads '1,5h' as fifteen hours
findings.detail: A comma is treated as a thousands separator, so one and a half hours written the way most of the world writes it becomes fifteen hours — a ten-fold error. timestring and @sapphire/duration do the same. The locale `decimal` option does not fix it.
findings.affectsYouIf: durations come from human-edited config and your users are not all using a dot as the decimal point

findings.headline: parse-duration drops the day from a valid ISO 8601 duration, and reads P1M as one minute
findings.detail: P1DT2H returns two hours; the day is gone. And P1M (one month) and PT1M (one minute) both return 60000, because M means months before the T and minutes after it. A monthly retention window becomes a one-minute one.
findings.affectsYouIf: you accept ISO 8601 durations from an API, a JSON Schema, or a calendar feed
findings.workaround: Parse ISO durations with a dedicated ISO parser.

findings.headline: croner fires an hourly job twice at the same instant across spring forward
findings.detail: '0 * * * *' in America/New_York on 2026-03-08 yields 24 fires for a 23-hour day, emitting 2026-03-08T07:00:00Z twice. cron-parser gives 23 for the same expression.
findings.affectsYouIf: you run sub-daily jobs in a timezone that observes daylight saving, and running twice is not safe
findings.workaround: Make the job idempotent, or use cron-parser to compute occurrences.

findings.headline: superjson silently loses five value kinds
findings.detail: Over 27 fixtures superjson returned a changed value without error for sparse arrays, null-prototype objects, ArrayBuffer, Error and class instances. devalue, measured on the same set, had zero silent losses: it is either exact or it throws.
findings.affectsYouIf: you send errors, class instances or binary data across a superjson boundary — a tRPC call, for instance
findings.workaround: Register a custom transformer for those types, or use devalue.

findings.headline: timestring returns a positive number for a negative duration
findings.affectsYouIf: durations in your system can be negative — an offset, a drift correction, a relative time
findings.workaround: Handle the sign yourself before parsing.

findings.headline: JSON.parse silently corrupts any integer past 2^53
findings.detail: Not a package defect — a property of the language that catches people constantly. A Discord or Twitter snowflake, a Postgres bigint or an amount in the smallest currency unit comes back as a different number with no error. Six of six tested payloads changed value.
findings.affectsYouIf: an API you consume returns 64-bit integer ids or amounts as JSON numbers
findings.workaround: Use lossless-json or json-bigint. Both were measured 8/8 correct.
